newCitations.caseName: Eden Brook Condominium, Inc. v. NVR, Inc. d/b/a Ryan Homes
newCitations.citation: Circuit Court for Anne Arundel County, Maryland, jury verdict Nov. 19, 2012
newCitations.outcome: Condo association for a 55-and-older community in Odenton, MD sued NVR (parent of Ryan Homes) for faulty construction after leaks forced some homeowners to keep buckets in their units, brickwork failed to meet industry standards, and undersized AC units caused chronic cooling problems; the association also alleged NVR misrepresented the quality of the buildings during construction and failed to maintain them. Attorneys interviewed 26 homeowners before filing suit in 2011. After a five-week trial, the jury awarded $5.6 million in compensatory damages -- against a $10 million ask in the complaint.
newCitations.notes: Older than the file's other citations but real, well-documented, multifamily (condo association, not single-family), and a useful mid-range full-trial verdict data point between the small subcontractor-defect cases and the nine/ten-figure catastrophic-collapse outliers already in the file.

newCitations.caseName: BML Properties Ltd. v. China Construction America, Inc. (Baha Mar Resort Litigation)
newCitations.citation: N.Y. Sup. Ct., Commercial Division (New York County), trial verdict Oct. 2024 (exact index number not independently confirmed from a primary court source)
newCitations.outcome: Developer BML Properties won a $1.6 billion trial verdict against China Construction America, Inc. (and related China State Construction entities) in New York's Commercial Division on fraud and breach-of-contract claims arising from the deeply troubled construction of the Baha Mar resort in Nassau, Bahamas -- a project plagued by years-long delays and defects that led to a bankruptcy filing before the resort finally opened.
newCitations.notes: Verified only via the prevailing law firm's own case-results page, not an independently pulled docket entry or reported opinion -- flagged accordingly. Framed as fraud + breach of contract rather than pure negligence, and the $1.6B figure includes fraud damages far beyond a repair-cost estimate, so it should be read as a new outlier ceiling for what a 'contractor breach' claim can be worth in the most egregious, bad-faith fact patterns -- not as a data point for calibrating the ordinary repairCostEstimate formula.

newCitations.caseName: Gallery Community Association v. K. Hovnanian at Gallery, LLC
newCitations.citation: No. 1 CA-CV 23-0375 (Ariz. Ct. App. 2024); review granted, Ariz. Sup. Ct. No. CV-24-0252-PR
newCitations.outcome: Developer Hovnanian built and sold eighteen townhomes and conveyed the common areas to a homeowners' association, which was also given control over exterior maintenance of the units. The trial court granted summary judgment to Hovnanian, holding the association held no implied warranty of workmanship/habitability because it did not own the residences. The Arizona Court of Appeals vacated that ruling, holding A.R.S. Sec. 33-2002(A) lets the association invoke the implied warranty to sue the developer over defects in common-area structures and in the exterior portions of homes it is obligated to maintain. The Arizona Supreme Court granted review in 2025/2026.
newCitations.notes: Not a damages case -- a standing/doctrine case -- but directly relevant to appliesIf logic: it expands WHO can bring a contractor-breach claim (a common-interest-community association, not just the unit owners individually) for common-area and exterior defects, in a state that had not previously settled the question. Still pending further review at the Arizona Supreme Court as of this research.

newCitations.caseName: 700 Edgewater Condominium Association, Inc. v. OKO Group, LLC et al. (Missoni Baia)
newCitations.citation: Miami-Dade County Circuit Court, Florida, filed Jan. 30, 2026
newCitations.outcome: Condo association for the 249-unit, 60-story Missoni Baia tower in Edgewater (Miami) sued developer OKO Group, design firms Asymptote and Revuelta, general contractor Civic Construction, and 19 subcontractors, alleging 76 separate construction and design defects -- cracked floor slabs and columns, water intrusion into units/stairwells/the parking garage, defective fire-alarm devices and sprinklers, leaking pool plumbing, missing hot water in parts of the tower, and non-functioning elevators. No damages figure has been pled yet; the case is at an early pleading stage.
newCitations.notes: Included for volume/severity of defect allegations in a recent large commercial high-rise, not for a dollar figure -- outcome is entirely undetermined at this stage. A companion suit (OKO Group v. its own insurers, seeking $22M) is pending over coverage for the same defects.

newCitations.caseName: Musallam / Veritas Capital Management, LLC v. Sapir / Americaribe-Moriarty (Arte Surfside Construction Defect Litigation)
newCitations.citation: Miami-Dade County Circuit Court, Florida, reported 2026 (exact filing date and index number not independently confirmed)
newCitations.outcome: The buyer of a penthouse at the Arte Surfside condominium (purchased for approximately $33 million in 2020) sued developer Alex Sapir and joint-venture general contractor Americaribe-Moriarty, alleging glass and glazing defects and a mechanical system that allows water intrusion, causing excessive condensation throughout the building. No damages figure or resolution has been publicly reported.
newCitations.notes: Secondary reporting only; no docket number independently verified and outcome fully pending. Included to round out the sample of currently-active South Florida high-rise construction-defect litigation, alongside Missoni Baia above.

newCitations.caseName: Mid-Century Insurance Co. v. HIVE Construction, Inc.
newCitations.outcome: HIVE Construction, general contractor for a Denver-area restaurant build-out, substituted plywood for one of two required layers of fire-rated drywall on a wall separating the kitchen and dining area, without seeking approval or a change order. A fire later started inside that wall, causing significant damage and forcing the restaurant to close. The property insurer, as subrogee, sued HIVE for negligence, alleging willful and wanton conduct. The Colorado Supreme Court held the economic loss rule bars the negligence claim because HIVE's duty not to deviate from the specified materials arose from the contract itself, not from an independent tort duty -- and that there is no willful-and-wanton exception to the economic loss rule in Colorado.
newCitations.notes: A defense-favorable limiting doctrine directly relevant to the 'negligence' half of this claim type's label: in economic-loss-rule states, a plaintiff confined to a contractual relationship with the contractor may be unable to plead a tort/negligence claim at all (even for reckless deviation from plans), win or lose on the facts -- pushing realistic probability toward the bottom of the current [0.55, 0.8] range whenever the claim is pled purely in tort in such a jurisdiction.

newCitations.caseName: Confidential Construction-Defect Arbitration re: 88-Unit Condominium, Palm Springs, CA
newCitations.citation: Private arbitration (mediation failed first), resolved late 2024; case name, arbitrator, and docket not publicly disclosed
newCitations.outcome: An 88-unit condominium association arbitrated construction-defect claims arising from vinyl window and sliding-glass-door frames that literally melted in the Palm Springs desert heat, plus failed deck waterproofing, corroded steel posts, significant stucco cracking, and water trapped behind stone veneer. The dispute settled/resolved in arbitration for $9.75 million.
newCitations.notes: Reported only via the prevailing law firm's own case-result page -- no independently verifiable case name or docket. Included anyway because it is a real, well-documented recent outcome consistent in magnitude with the file's other post-occupancy latent-defect entries (roughly $111,000/unit here, in the same order of magnitude as Park Hill's per-unit figure), and because confidential arbitration -- not a published opinion -- is how a large share of real-world commercial construction-defect disputes actually resolve.

contractor_breach_negligence.calibrationNote: The expanded sample does not push the current baseProbability [0.55, 0.8] in either direction, but it does surface two real considerations the model doesn't yet capture. First, Baha Mar's $1.6B verdict and the Eden Brook $5.6M jury verdict (56% of the $10M ask) both support plaintiffs recovering at real scale on strong facts, consistent with the current top-of-range confidence. Second, and more important, Mid-Century v. HIVE shows that in economic-loss-rule jurisdictions a purely tort-framed negligence claim against a contractor can be barred outright regardless of the facts -- since this claim type's label is 'Contractor Breach / Negligence,' the probability should arguably be modeled slightly lower when the fact pattern is negligence-only (no separate contract claim) and the project state follows a strict economic-loss rule. The range itself still looks right as a blended average across contract and tort framings.

newCitations.caseName: Nantucket Cottage Hospital v. CannonDesign, Inc.
newCitations.citation: Suffolk Superior Court, Massachusetts, complaint filed June 2023 (exact docket number not independently confirmed)
newCitations.outcome: The hospital sued its architect, CannonDesign, for breach of contract, negligence, and malpractice over the design of its new facility (opened 2019), alleging Cannon designed non-load-bearing exterior walls using flammable cedar shingles to satisfy the local Historic District Commission -- a fire-code violation that prevented the hospital from obtaining full Medicare/Medicaid licensure and forced it to operate under temporary waivers while redesigning and rebuilding the walls at a cost of millions. The hospital sought at least $8 million. No settlement or judgment has been located in available reporting.
newCitations.notes: Outcome undisclosed/unconfirmed -- treat the $8M figure as the amount sought, not a resolved recovery.

newCitations.caseName: Bozzuto affiliate v. Icon Architecture, Inc. (The Abby, North Quincy)
newCitations.citation: Massachusetts state court, filed April 2024 (exact venue/docket number not independently confirmed)
newCitations.outcome: A Bozzuto affiliate sued Boston-based Icon Architecture over dozens of alleged design errors at The Abby, a 610-unit mixed-use development next to the North Quincy MBTA station, claiming more than $3 million in resulting damages. Among the specific errors alleged: construction drawings for elevator pits in two buildings failed to specify code-required sump pumps, requiring demolition and re-pour of already-completed concrete slabs. Icon's president publicly disputed the allegations. Outcome/resolution not yet reported.
newCitations.notes: A large, recent, commercial multifamily design-error claim with a specific, verifiable defect mechanism (missing sump-pump specification) rather than a vague 'design was bad' allegation -- useful even though pending.

newCitations.caseName: Wold v. Select Structural Engineering, LLC (Davenport, Iowa Building Collapse Litigation)
newCitations.citation: Scott County District Court, Iowa (multiple related actions filed and consolidated in 2023; individual docket numbers not independently confirmed)
newCitations.outcome: A 116-year-old mixed-use/apartment building at 324 Main St. in Davenport partially collapsed on May 28, 2023, killing three residents and displacing roughly 100 households. Building owner Andrew Wold had retained Select Structural Engineering to inspect the building and advise on repairs; Wold sued the firm for negligence and breach of contract, alleging it advised the building was not in danger despite noting wall damage during inspection. Select Structural counterclaimed against Wold and Davenport Hotel LLC, alleging dozens of its own claims including negligence and contribution. At least six related lawsuits (including from injured/displaced residents) were filed and consolidated. Outcome undisclosed as of available reporting.
newCitations.notes: The most severe design/inspection-malpractice fact pattern found for this claim type -- deaths and mass displacement, comparable in severity to the catastrophicLifeSafetyFailure tier already used for contractor_breach_negligence -- but here the alleged malpractice is against a structural engineering/inspection firm rather than a general contractor. No dollar outcome available, but it confirms this claim type can reach the same top-of-range severity as the contractor-side claim, not only the mid-size redesign-cost claims the current sample otherwise reflects.

newCitations.caseName: Barefoot Resort Residential Owners Association v. D3G Architects, Wingate Consulting Engineers, UFP Mid-Atlantic, JM Allen Construction, and Excel Custom Builders
newCitations.citation: Horry County, South Carolina state court, filed Aug. 11, 2020 (exact case number not independently confirmed)
newCitations.outcome: A homeowners association sued five defendants -- including architect D3G and engineer Wingate Consulting -- over a $1.5 million beach cabana project at a North Myrtle Beach resort, identifying 13 alleged construction and design defects, most notably the substitution of galvanized steel for specified stainless-steel building hangers and truss plates (workers attempted to coat the galvanized steel rather than replace it), plus improper laminated-veneer-lumber beams, incompatible anchors, and defective concrete-block column construction. The association terminated its contracts with the architect and general contractor, hired replacements, and proceeded with the project while litigation continued. Final resolution not confirmed in available reporting.
newCitations.notes: An older filing with no confirmed final outcome, but factually rich on the design/spec-substitution mechanism and useful as a smaller-project, commercial-amenity data point distinct from the campus/institutional-building fact patterns that dominate this claim type's existing sample.

design_professional_malpractice.calibrationNote: All four new citations are still pending or have undisclosed final outcomes -- none of them adds a single new CONFIRMED dollar resolution to the sample, which by itself is informative: 5 of the file's 6 total design-malpractice citations now lack a confirmed final number, versus a much higher confirmed-outcome rate for the contractor_breach_negligence and indemnification samples. That reinforces, rather than undermines, the existing note's core finding that design-malpractice claims resolve unusually slowly and often confidentially. Recommend leaving baseProbability [0.35, 0.6] unchanged, but flagging in documentation that confidence in this claim type's calibration is structurally lower than for the other three construction-defect claim types simply because so few real outcomes become public.

newCitations.outcome: General contractor Fortune-Johnson was sued for breach of contract over construction of an apartment building and, in turn, filed separate indemnification actions against each of its subcontractors. The Virginia Court of Appeals held the subcontracts' primary indemnity clause was void under Va. Code Sec. 11-4.1 because it expressly required the subcontractors to indemnify the general contractor for the general contractor's OWN negligence -- an obligation the statute squarely prohibits -- and rejected the contractor's argument that the clause's 'to the fullest extent permitted by law' language saved it, holding Virginia courts lack authority to blue-pencil an overbroad indemnity provision into an enforceable one.
newCitations.notes: Commercial multifamily (apartment building) fact pattern. Directly confirms the file's existing constructionIndemnityStateModifiers treatment of Virginia-style anti-indemnity statutes: an improperly broad clause is VOIDED outright (no partial enforcement/reformation), not merely narrowed to a proportionate-fault ceiling.

newCitations.caseName: Dibrino v. Rockefeller Center North, Inc.
newCitations.outcome: A worker fell from a ladder that had been left open and unattended by an employee of DAL Electrical Corporation, the electrical subcontractor on a Rockefeller Center-area project where Rockefeller Center North, Inc. was the owner and JRM Construction Management LLC was the construction manager/general contractor. The New York Court of Appeals held DAL owed no contractual indemnity to the owner or GC because the injury did not 'arise out of, or result from,' the performance of DAL's own contracted electrical work -- and refused to fall back on a broader indemnity clause elsewhere in the same contract, reasoning that doing so would render the narrower, more specific indemnity provision meaningless.
newCitations.notes: A very recent, high-profile New York Court of Appeals decision on a commercial building. Key addition to the model: it shows a facially enforceable indemnity clause can still fail on CAUSATION/SCOPE grounds (whether the claim 'arises out of' the indemnitor's specific work) -- a distinct failure mode from the enforceability-ceiling logic (indemnityForm: limited/intermediate/broad) that the state-law modifier currently captures.

newCitations.caseName: Seneca Specialty Insurance Co. v. Jade Beach Condominium Association, Inc.
newCitations.outcome: After a unit owner sued the Jade Beach condominium association and two construction companies, the association's insurer, Seneca, paid the association $1 million under its policy. The association then settled with and released the construction-defect defendants. Seneca sued the association for breach of contract, alleging the releases impaired Seneca's subrogation/contribution rights against those construction defendants. The trial court dismissed Seneca's suit as premature, reasoning Seneca first had to sue the released construction defendants itself and obtain a judgment establishing impairment. The Third District Court of Appeal reversed, holding the policy did not require the insurer to sue the released parties first before pursuing its own breach-of-contract claim against its insured.
newCitations.notes: Not a GC-vs-subcontractor indemnification fight -- an insurer-vs-insured dispute over whether the insured association's own settlement with the underlying construction-defect tortfeasors improperly extinguished the carrier's contribution/subrogation rights. Directly relevant to any owner/association negotiating a global construction-defect settlement while a property or liability carrier has already paid out: releasing the contractors without protecting the carrier's contribution rights can itself become a second, independent claim.

newCitations.caseName: 450 Gin Lane SH, LLC v. Gentry Constr. Co., Inc.
newCitations.outcome: An owner sued general contractor Gentry for breach of contract, alleging its work on a residence failed to comply with codes, plans, and specifications. Gentry brought a third-party action against sub-subcontractors D&C and Shope seeking common-law indemnification and contribution. The Appellate Division affirmed dismissal of Gentry's common-law indemnification claim against both, holding common-law indemnification is available only where the indemnitee's own conduct is 'solely passive' and its potential liability purely vicarious -- and here the owner's complaint alleged Gentry's OWN failure to construct the project according to the required standards, precluding common-law indemnification regardless of what D&C's and Shope's subcontracts said.
newCitations.notes: CAVEAT: the underlying project here was a single-family residence, not commercial/multifamily -- included despite that because the holding restates a live, currently-litigated New York rule with obvious commercial application: where a construction-defect plaintiff alleges the GC's OWN failure to build to spec (the typical construction-defect pleading), COMMON-LAW indemnification against downstream subs is categorically unavailable no matter how the sub-subcontracts are worded -- a failure mode distinct from, and not currently modeled alongside, the contractual-indemnity-ceiling logic already in the file.

indemnification_contribution_claim.calibrationNote: The state-law-modifier approach (indemnityForm ceiling by jurisdiction) is confirmed as directionally correct by Fortune-Johnson, which shows Virginia's anti-indemnity statute voiding an improperly broad clause exactly as the model would predict. But three of the four new citations (Dibrino, Seneca/Jade Beach, 450 Gin Lane) turn on a SECOND variable the model doesn't currently isolate: even a facially enforceable clause can fail on causation/scope-of-work grounds, and common-law (non-contractual) indemnification fails categorically whenever the indemnitee's own conduct is directly at issue rather than purely vicarious. BaseProbability [0.4, 0.7] is still a reasonable blended range, but consider noting that the ceiling-only state-law modifier likely overstates recovery odds in cases where causation/scope or the passive-vicarious-liability requirement is contested, independent of which state's indemnity-form rule applies.

newCitations.caseName: Acuity, a Mutual Insurance Co. v. M/I Homes of Chicago, LLC
newCitations.outcome: A townhome owners' association sued developer M/I Homes for breach of contract and breach of the implied warranty of habitability, alleging M/I's subcontractors caused construction defects through defective materials, faulty workmanship, and code violations. M/I demanded a defense from Acuity as an additional insured under a subcontractor's CGL policy; Acuity sought a declaratory judgment that the underlying complaint alleged no 'property damage' caused by an 'occurrence.' The trial court agreed with Acuity and found no duty to defend. The Illinois Supreme Court reversed in relevant part, holding that negligent subcontractor work causing damage to the project can constitute 'property damage' caused by an 'occurrence' under a standard CGL policy -- expressly overruling prior Illinois appellate precedent that had treated construction-defect claims as categorically uninsurable business-risk exclusions.
newCitations.notes: A landmark, widely-cited decision that materially EXPANDS CGL coverage availability for construction-defect claims in a major jurisdiction, reversing a more insurer-favorable prior rule. Underlying claim was a residential townhome HOA dispute, but the coverage holding applies with equal force to commercial CGL disputes and should be treated as a real doctrinal shift pushing Illinois-sited claims toward the higher end of the coverage-probability range.

newCitations.caseName: Lessard v. R.C. Havens & Sons, Inc.
newCitations.outcome: After homeowners won a jury verdict against homebuilder R.C. Havens & Sons over construction defects, the homebuilder's CGL insurer intervened seeking a declaration it owed no duty to indemnify. The Massachusetts Appeals Court held that the cost of repairing or removing a construction defect ITSELF is not 'property damage' within the meaning of a CGL policy, but the cost of repairing damage CAUSED BY that defect to otherwise non-defective work or property IS covered 'property damage' -- a split, partially insurer-favorable holding rather than a clean win for either side.
newCitations.notes: Underlying dispute was residential (homebuilder/homeowner), included because the defect-repair-cost-vs-resulting-damage-cost distinction is one of the most heavily litigated CGL construction-defect coverage issues nationally and directly bears on the file's coveredPortionOfUnderlyingDefectDamages formula -- that formula likely should already discount for the slice of repair cost attributable to the defect itself, since that slice is frequently uninsured even where a duty to defend/broader coverage exists.

newCitations.caseName: Westchester Modular Homes of Fairfield County, Inc. v. Arbella Protection Ins. Co.
newCitations.outcome: A contractor sued its own CGL insurer, Arbella, to recover defense costs incurred in an underlying construction-defect action alleging water intrusion. The Connecticut Appellate Court held that water intrusion alone, without resulting damage to other property, does not constitute 'property damage' caused by an 'occurrence' under the CGL policy -- an insurer-favorable ruling limiting the contractor's ability to recover its defense costs for that portion of the underlying claim.
newCitations.notes: Based on secondary case-summary reporting rather than a full read of the opinion text -- flagged accordingly. Consistent with the general national trend (also seen in Lessard) of appellate courts narrowing what counts as covered 'property damage' in pure water-intrusion/defect-only fact patterns.

newCitations.caseName: The Travelers Indemnity Co. of Connecticut v. I.C. Refrigeration Service, Inc. et al.
newCitations.citation: Order filed Nov. 10, 2025, U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California (case/docket number not independently confirmed beyond the CourtListener docket entry)
newCitations.outcome: Travelers sought a declaratory judgment that it owed no duty to defend or indemnify its insureds, I.C. Refrigeration Service and Flory Construction, in a construction-defect action brought against them by project owner Highbridge Oakland. The court granted the insureds' motion to dismiss Travelers' duty-to-defend claim, holding Travelers could not show the damages Highbridge sought were not potentially covered 'property damage,' and stayed the remaining duty-to-indemnify claim pending resolution of the underlying suit. The court separately denied, without prejudice, Travelers' later motion for default judgment seeking a declaration that the damages alleged were purely economic rather than property damage.
newCitations.notes: An interim/procedural ruling (motion to dismiss plus a denied default-judgment motion), not a final coverage determination -- included as a very recent, real data point showing insurers still frequently losing duty-to-defend declaratory actions at the pleading stage whenever the underlying complaint is pled broadly enough to allege potentially-covered property damage.

insurance_coverage_defect_dispute.calibrationNote: The existing note's framing -- coverage litigation resolves a legal yes/no question while the dollar consequences flow through separate, often confidential settlements -- holds up well against the expanded sample: none of the four new citations produces a clean dollar recovery figure either. The outcomes also split roughly evenly in direction (Acuity is policyholder/additional-insured-favorable; Lessard and Westchester Modular are insurer-favorable or mixed; Travelers is a procedural insurer loss but not a final coverage ruling), which supports leaving baseProbability [0.45, 0.65] unchanged as a genuinely close-to-even range rather than adjusting it in either direction. Continue treating this claim type's output as a coverage-likelihood signal rather than a reliable dollar estimate.
